bergson: Henri Bergson (1859–1941) was a French philosopher of time, memory, and creative evolution, awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature. He argued that lived time—duration (durée)—flows and cannot be captured by clocks or concepts, and his theory of laughter held that we find things comic when something mechanical encroaches on the living.
cs-lewis: C.S. Lewis (1898–1963) was a British literary scholar and novelist, best known for the Narnia books, who became one of the twentieth century's most influential Christian thinkers. His popular works on faith and reason, the problem of pain, and different kinds of love gave ordinary readers accessible arguments for Christian belief.
deleuze: Gilles Deleuze (1925–1995) was a French post-structuralist philosopher who, with psychoanalyst Félix Guattari, reworked the Freudian unconscious into a theory of flows of desire. He is best known for the rhizome—a non-hierarchical, endlessly branching model of thought and culture that opposes tree-like hierarchies.
diogenes-cynic: Diogenes the Cynic (c. 412–323 BC) was a Greek philosopher famous for living in a large jar and carrying a lamp in daylight, 'looking for an honest man.' He advocated living according to nature, rejecting wealth, status, and social convention as corrupting—shock tactics meant to teach virtue by example.
donald-davidson: Donald Davidson (1917–2003) was a major American analytic philosopher who argued that mind, language, and action must be understood together. He developed a truth-based theory of meaning and radical interpretation, and defended a form of compatibilism on which free action is action done from one's own desires and reasons.
frege: Gottlob Frege (1848–1925) was a German logician widely regarded as the founder of modern logic and analytic philosophy. His distinction between sense and reference transformed thinking about meaning, and his attempt to ground arithmetic in logic shaped the philosophy of mathematics.
freud: Sigmund Freud (1856–1939) was the Austrian founder of psychoanalysis. He argued that an unconscious mind, filled with repressed desires, shapes our conscious lives; his later theory of the death drive and his account of civilization as a bargain trading instinctual freedom for security remain hugely influential, though his scientific status is contested.
husserl: Edmund Husserl (1859–1938) was an Austrian-German philosopher and founder of phenomenology, the study of the structures of lived experience. His central idea of intentionality—that consciousness is always consciousness of something—and his method of 'bracketing' assumptions profoundly shaped Heidegger, Sartre, and Merleau-Ponty.
kripke: Saul Kripke (1940–2022) was an American logician and analytic philosopher whose Naming and Necessity revolutionized philosophy of language. Arguing that proper names are 'rigid designators' that pick out the same object in every possible world, he restored necessity to philosophy and reopened mind–body questions.
lacan: Jacques Lacan (1901–1981) was a French psychoanalyst who reread Freud through structural linguistics, famously declaring that 'the unconscious is structured like a language.' His mirror stage—the infant's first image of itself as a whole self—and his triad of the Imaginary, Symbolic, and Real became staples of continental thought.
levinas: Emmanuel Levinas (1906–1995) was a Lithuanian-born French phenomenologist who placed ethics before all other philosophy. He argued that the face of the Other presents an immediate, unchosen demand: 'you shall not kill.' Human responsibility for others, not self-knowledge or freedom, is where philosophy must begin.
mackinnon: Catharine MacKinnon (b. 1946) is an American radical feminist legal scholar who argues that gender inequality is built into sexuality itself. Her 'dominance approach' treats pornography not as speech but as a central practice of women's subordination, and she helped draft anti-pornography ordinances (later struck down in court) with Andrea Dworkin.
marcuse: Herbert Marcuse (1898–1979) was a German-American member of the Frankfurt School who fused Marx and Freud. In One-Dimensional Man he argued that advanced consumer society satisfies needs just enough to absorb dissent and flatten critical thought, a diagnosis that made him a guru of the 1960s New Left.
moore: G.E. Moore (1873–1958) was a British philosopher at Cambridge and a founder of analytic philosophy. In Principia Ethica he charged that identifying 'good' with anything natural (like pleasure) commits the naturalistic fallacy, and his 'here is one hand' arguments made him a famous, deadpan opponent of skepticism about the external world.
nagel: Thomas Nagel (b. 1937) is an American philosopher best known for asking 'What is it like to be a bat?', which argues that subjective experience resists any purely physical description. He has also written influentially on the absurd, moral luck, and death, in essays admired for combining rigor with candor.
protagoras: Protagoras (c. 490–420 BC) was the most celebrated of the Greek Sophists, itinerant teachers of rhetoric and argument. His dictum that 'man is the measure of all things' made him the classic relativist: what seems true or good to each person is true or good for that person.
pyrrho: Pyrrho (c. 360–270 BC) was a Greek philosopher, traditionally the founder of Pyrrhonian skepticism. He taught that we should suspend judgment on all non-obvious claims, holding that things are no more this than that—and that this suspension of judgment brings the peace of mind the skeptics called tranquility.
pythagoras: Pythagoras (c. 570–495 BC) was a Greek mystic and mathematician whose brotherhood of followers discovered that musical harmony depends on simple number ratios. His doctrine that number is the key to reality and his belief in the transmigration of souls deeply influenced Plato, though the facts of his life are hard to separate from legend.
rudolf-carnap: Rudolf Carnap (1891–1970) was a German-born philosopher and leading member of the Vienna Circle, the movement of logical positivists. He championed the verifiability principle—the view that a statement is meaningful only if empirically testable or purely logical—and the idea that scientific theories are languages we choose between.
ryle: Gilbert Ryle (1900–1976) was an Oxford philosopher whose The Concept of Mind ridiculed Cartesian dualism as 'the ghost in the machine'—the mistake of treating the mind as a hidden thing inside the body. He argued instead that mental life is shown in intelligent behavior, and in knowing-how as much as knowing-that.
tocqueville: Alexis de Tocqueville (1805–1859) was a French political thinker whose Democracy in America, based on his travels, remains a classic analysis of democracy's strengths and dangers. He warned that democratic equality could breed a 'tyranny of the majority' and a soft, administrative despotism, and saw local associations as democracy's saving grace.
turing: Alan Turing (1912–1954) was a British mathematician, wartime codebreaker, and founding father of computer science. His proposed 'imitation game'—now the Turing Test—posed the question of whether machines can think, framing debates about artificial intelligence and the mind that continue today.
whitehead: Alfred North Whitehead (1861–1947) was a British mathematician-philosopher who, after co-authoring Principia Mathematica with Russell, founded process philosophy: the view that reality consists not of static substances but of events and becomings. He rejected the 'fallacy of misplaced concreteness'—mistaking abstractions for the concrete world—and built a metaphysics in which God himself evolves with the world.
zhuangzi: Zhuangzi (c. 369–286 BC) was a Chinese Daoist philosopher, the second great figure of Daoism after Laozi. His playful, parable-filled book—famous for the butterfly dream, in which he wakes unsure whether he is a man who dreamt he was a butterfly—argues that perspectives are relative and that wisdom lies in spontaneous, effortless action.
